content: During discussions and decision-making processes regarding language, the strength of recommendations and the quality of evidence were carefully considered. Throughout the meeting, WHO staff consistently emphasized the principles and guidelines that underpin the WHO decision-making process. The Guideline Development Group reached a consensus on all recommendations after revising the text. The recommendations concerning the duration of breastfeeding by mothers living with HIV were extensively debated to achieve agreement on the strength of the recommendations. Voting was used solely as a straw-poll method to gauge consensus, and no decisions were subjected to a final vote. The Guideline Development Group chose not to make recommendations in all cases but instead formulated guiding practice statements using the same methodological approach. The WHO Steering Committee circulated the draft recommendations to an External Peer Review Group, which provided several suggestions to enhance the document. These suggestions were reviewed by the WHO Steering Committee and incorporated as appropriate after discussions and agreement with the chair and co-chair of the Guideline Development Group. No new recommendations were considered during this round of comments, and the final version was approved by the Guideline Development Group. The recommendations in this guideline will be disseminated through a wide network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, health ministries, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. They will also be published on the WHO website and the websites of partner agencies. To ensure the guideline reaches the intended users, WHO will organize meetings with key stakeholders in settings with a high prevalence of HIV and present the recommendations at international AIDS and infant feeding conferences. Assistance will be provided to adapt the guideline to national contexts as needed. The Guideline Development Group emphasized the importance of clarifying the changes included in the recommendations and commenting on what remained unchanged. They also highlighted the need to support communities in understanding the recommendations, which would involve simplifying messages. Coordination with other health programs, including HIV programs on antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and general maternal and child health programs, will be essential. The initial steps in implementing this guideline after final approval will involve revising all WHO publications that address populations of pregnant women, mothers, and infants for whom the recommendations may have implications. WHO will collaborate with health ministries and established partners involved in training, capacity development related to HIV and infant feeding, and supervision of health workers at first-level health facilities. The successful introduction of evidence-informed policies supporting infant feeding practices by mothers living with HIV into national programs and healthcare services will depend on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. These processes may include developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols based on this document and undergraduate and in-service teaching curricula. Individual countries are expected to adapt the recommendations to suit their local social, cultural, and economic contexts. Countries will be encouraged to hold discussions with key stakeholders to inform decision-making on using and introducing the recommendations into national programs. Frameworks to assist policymakers, such as DECIDE (Developing and Evaluating Communication Strategies to Support Informed Decisions and Practice based on Evidence), will be shared. The recommendations in this guideline should be adapted into locally appropriate documents to meet the specific needs of each country and health service. An enabling environment should be created for the use of these recommendations, including relevant national policies and changes in the behavior of healthcare practitioners to facilitate evidence-informed practices. Local professional societies may play significant roles in this process, and an inclusive and participatory approach should be encouraged. WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health, Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, and Department of HIV have substantial experience introducing WHO guidelines and tools into national programs. Within this context, program managers must ensure that adequate quantities of required ARV drugs are available to health workers and mothers living with HIV. These drugs would typically be provided through existing health system supply chains. Monitoring and evaluation should be integrated into the implementation process to provide valuable lessons for uptake and further implementation. Priority should be given to strong recommendations when monitoring and evaluating their impact on the quality of care. The implementation of this guideline should involve national child health programs collecting and reporting data on pregnant women and mothers living with HIV and their exposed newborns. This may require reviewing existing patient monitoring systems, including reporting tools, to ensure that the conditions are adequately addressed. Key areas requiring monitoring include, but are not limited to: Infant feeding practices by mothers living with HIV, including the duration of breastfeeding. ART coverage among mothers living with HIV. Growth among infants and children being breastfed by mothers living with HIV who are taking ART. WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health, Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, and Department of HIV will monitor the implementation of the guideline in collaboration with WHO regional and country offices. Indicators such as the number of requests from countries for technical assistance in implementing the guideline and requests to WHO headquarters and regional offices for monitoring and evaluation in countries applying the guideline will be used. Additionally, the number of downloads of the guideline publication from the WHO website and those of partners and other stakeholders, as well as the number of hard copies requested and distributed through the WHO document center, will be monitored. Several specific clinical and programmatic research questions were identified during discussions on individual recommendations, and these are included in the summary for each recommendation. Implementation research will also inform and assist the adoption of policy and implementation. Facilitating policy adoption and creating an enabling environment for implementation will require dialogue with policymakers and other stakeholders at the country level. Program managers will need technical support for developing and implementing operational plans in program settings from experts experienced in delivering these interventions. Small-scale demonstration projects may support designing and scaling up training, capacity development, and implementation at the country level. This guideline will be reviewed in 2019. At that time, the WHO Steering Committee will convene a Guideline Development Group to review the literature and update the recommendations as needed. In the interim, the WHO Steering Committee will continue to monitor any new studies, interim research results, or reports of adverse events associated with this policy implementation that become available. If relevant new information necessitates urgent changes to the recommendations before 2019, a Guideline Development Group will be convened in accordance with the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development.
